summary: Defines an experimental extension to IMAP that lets clients and servers store metadata, such as comments or flags, on whole messages or on individual message parts kept in a server mailbox. It was published as Experimental because the working group wanted implementation and deployment experience before moving toward a standards-track version, and it warns that later versions may change incompatibly.

eli5.summary: It is like sticky notes you can attach to a letter in a filing cabinet. The notes stay with the letter on the server, so any of your devices can read them later.

questions: how to attach comments to email messages on imap server
how to store comments on imap messages
subtitle: How an IMAP server can store comments, flags and other notes on messages and on individual message parts.

tldr.problem: IMAP has no standard way to attach extra information, such as a comment or a per-part flag, to a message stored on the server, so every client keeps its own notes locally.
tldr.mechanism: The ANNOTATE extension gives each message named entries made of attributes, each stored as a private or a shared version, and adds FETCH, STORE, APPEND, SEARCH and SORT support for them.
tldr.outcome: It was published as Experimental because the working group wanted implementation and deployment experience first; a later standards-track version could change incompatibly under a new capability name.

today: RFC 5257 is an Experimental RFC, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text itself says the working group wanted implementation and deployment experience, and that a later standards-track version would use a new capability name if it changed incompatibly.

sections.title: What the ANNOTATE Extension Adds
sections.content:
The ANNOTATE extension lets clients and servers keep "meta data" for messages, or for individual message parts, in a mailbox on an IMAP server. A typical use is attaching a comment to a message. A server supports it when it returns ANNOTATE-EXPERIMENT-1 in its CAPABILITY response.

The extension adds a new ANNOTATION item to FETCH, STORE, APPEND, SEARCH and SORT, a new requirement on COPY, an ANNOTATE parameter for SELECT and EXAMINE, and new response codes. It also adds a new ACL right for the ACL extensions. The data model is based on the Application Configuration Access Protocol (RFC 2244), and annotations have no inheritance.

A server that supports annotations MUST store them permanently. There are no "session only" annotations. Servers SHOULD also support Conditional STORE (RFC 4551) so that disconnected clients can synchronize annotations well.
sections.eli5: Normally a mail server only keeps your letters. This adds a way to stick small notes on a letter or on one page of it, and the server keeps those notes for good.

sections.title: Entries, Attributes and Names
sections.content:
Each annotation is a uniquely named entry made of attributes. A comment on a whole message is the entry /comment, and it carries attributes such as value and size. A message may hold zero or more entries. Entry names use / to separate components and attribute names use .. Names are case-sensitive, ASCII only, and may not contain the asterisk or percent characters.

The value attribute holds the data, either a string or binary data, and storing NIL deletes it. The size attribute is set by the server and is read-only to clients. Entries that start with a digit refer to a body part, for example /<section-part>/comment. Other entries cover the whole message.

The RFC defines /comment, /altsubject (text the recipient wants shown instead of the original Subject) and vendor entries under /vendor/<vendor-token>. The /flags hierarchy is reserved for future use. Per body part there are flags/seen, flags/answered, flags/flagged and flags/forwarded, whose value is 1, 0 or NIL. The extension does not expose the normal IMAP flags as entries.
sections.eli5: Each note has a name, like a label on a drawer, and the drawer holds the note text and its size. Notes can be about the whole letter or about one page of it.

sections.title: Private, Shared and Who May Write
sections.content:
Every attribute name implicitly has a .priv and a .shared form. In a shared mailbox, shared annotations let a team add information to messages, for example on a folder of bug reports. Private ones let each person keep their own notes. If a FETCH or SEARCH names neither suffix it covers both, but STORE, APPEND and SORT MUST name one.

Servers are REQUIRED to support shared annotations. Private ones are OPTIONAL for servers, because tracking ownership and quota is more complex. Clients MUST handle both.

Without the ACL extension, access depends on whether the mailbox was opened read-write or read-only. With ACL, the r right controls reading of both kinds and writing of .priv values, and the new n right controls writing of .shared values. A client without the right gets a NO response.
sections.eli5: A private note is like a note in your own pocket that only you see. A shared note is pinned to the board where the whole team can read it.

sections.title: Commands and Responses
sections.content:
On SELECT or EXAMINE the server MUST return an ANNOTATIONS response code. Its values are NONE, READ-ONLY, NOPRIVATE or a number giving the largest value size in octets. If annotations can be written, servers MUST accept values of at least 1024 octets, and MUST allow at least 10 annotations per message. Adding the ANNOTATE parameter to SELECT turns on unsolicited updates that name a changed entry but never include its value.

FETCH takes an entry specifier and an attribute specifier, and the asterisk and percent characters work as wildcards in entry specifiers (percent does not cross the slash separator). STORE sets or replaces attributes and has an implicit .SILENT behavior. If a value is too big the server returns NO with [ANNOTATE TOOBIG], and if the per-message limit is reached it returns NO with [ANNOTATE TOOMANY].

APPEND can attach annotations to a new message. COPY MUST carry the current user's .priv data and all .shared data to the destination, unless the destination cannot hold them. SEARCH can match text in the value attributes, and SORT can sort on value.priv or value.shared of one fully named entry.
sections.eli5: The server tells you how big your notes may be and how many fit on one letter. You can then add, read, copy, search and sort by these notes just like other mail things.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The one specific warning is that annotations meant to stay private MUST be stored in .priv values, because .shared values may be visible to other users. Apart from that, the RFC says the extension raises no security issues beyond those of base IMAP (RFC 3501).

For text, servers MUST follow normal IMAP text normalization, character set conversion and collation rules when searching or sorting annotation values.
sections.eli5: If a note is secret, put it in the private pile. Anything in the shared pile may be seen by other people.

viz.caption: A FETCH EXAMPLE FROM THE RFC

data.title: Fetching a comment
data.code:
C: a FETCH 1 (ANNOTATION (/comment value))
S: * 1 FETCH (ANNOTATION (/comment
                           (value.priv "My comment"
                            value.shared NIL)))
S: a OK Fetch complete
